label: Smooth Manifolds
notes: Welcome to Chapter 1, spanning printed pages 1 through 31. We are building the central object of the whole course: a space that supports calculus without sitting inside any ambient Euclidean space. Today's layers are topology, charts, transition maps, smooth atlases, the maximal structure, examples, and boundary.

label: Topological Manifold
notes: A topological manifold rests on three pillars: locally Euclidean of fixed dimension, Hausdorff, and second-countable. Stress that locally Euclidean alone is too weak. The two global hypotheses rule out pathologies like the line with two origins and guarantee partitions of unity later, so do not treat them as decoration.

label: Why Hausdorff and Second-Countable
notes: Walk students through the two safeguards concretely. The line with two origins is locally Euclidean and second-countable yet fails Hausdorff, so limits are not unique. Second-countability bounds the number of charts and yields paracompactness. Both conditions are exactly what later integration and partition-of-unity arguments will require.

label: Coordinate Charts
notes: A chart is a homeomorphism from an open set of the manifold onto an open set of Euclidean space. Emphasize that the component functions are the local coordinates in which every future derivative, tangent vector, and form will be computed. A chart is the working coordinate system, not a mere label on a neighborhood.

label: Transition Maps
notes: When two charts overlap, composing one with the inverse of the other gives a transition map between open subsets of Euclidean space. This is an honest map you can differentiate. The entire smoothness question reduces to the regularity of these overlap maps, so train students to always inspect the overlap, never just each chart alone.

label: Smooth Atlas
notes: A smooth atlas is a collection of charts covering the manifold whose every pairwise transition map is infinitely differentiable. Charts whose overlap transition is smooth are called smoothly compatible. The atlas is the package of data that finally lets us say a function or map between manifolds is itself smooth.

label: Smooth Structure
notes: Two smooth atlases that are compatible determine the same calculus, so we pass to the maximal atlas, the union of all compatible charts. This maximal atlas is the smooth structure. Maximality removes any dependence on an arbitrary finite list of charts and makes the smooth manifold a well-defined object.

label: Compatibility Can Fail
notes: Compatibility is a genuine condition, not automatic. On the real line the standard coordinate and the cube coordinate u equals x cubed each give a smooth one-chart atlas, but the reverse change x equals u to the one-third has unbounded derivative at zero. So these two atlases are smooth yet mutually incompatible.

label: The Sphere by Stereographic Charts
notes: The sphere is the model example. Stereographic projection from the north pole charts everything but that pole, and projection from the south pole charts everything but the other. Their overlap transition is inversion, which is smooth away from the origin. Two charts, smoothly glued, give the sphere its standard smooth structure.

label: A Gallery of Examples
notes: Survey the constructions that recur all term: Euclidean space itself, graphs of smooth functions, spheres as regular level sets, real and complex projective spaces as quotients, products of manifolds, open matrix groups like the general linear group, and Grassmannians. Each one is verified by the same local-coordinate plus smooth-transition logic.

label: Projective Spaces and Grassmannians
notes: Projective space identifies nonzero vectors that differ by a scalar; its standard charts are the affine patches where one homogeneous coordinate is nonzero. Grassmannians generalize this to k-dimensional subspaces, charted by graphs over a fixed complement. Both inherit Hausdorff, second-countable smooth structures from these explicit overlapping charts.

label: Manifolds with Boundary
notes: To allow edges we change the local model from open subsets of Euclidean space to open subsets of the closed half-space. Points hitting the bounding hyperplane are boundary points; the rest are interior. Boundary status is intrinsic, invariant under smooth charts, and the boundary is itself a manifold of one lower dimension.

label: Classifier and Recap
notes: We close with a diagnostic checklist applied to candidate spaces. A space fails when it is not locally Euclidean, mixes dimensions, separates points poorly, or carries incompatible charts. Recap the layered model: topology first, smooth compatibility second, examples and boundary built from the same overlap logic that drives all later calculus.
